english: in advance, ahead of time, beforehand
usage: The single most useful collocation for residents; pairs with 식당, 호텔, 병원
to say ahead of time / give notice
Used for advance notice; 미리 말해 주세요 = please tell me beforehand
The default verb after 미리; 서류를 미리 준비하다 = prep documents early
well in advance, in good time
Doubled form stressing 'nice and early, with margin to spare'
examples: 표를 미리 샀어요.
I bought the tickets in advance.
Simplest frame: 미리 + buy, the early-action core meaning
인기 식당은 미리 예약하지 않으면 자리가 없어요.
Popular restaurants have no seats unless you reserve in advance.
Everyday: 미리 + 예약하다 in a -지 않으면 conditional, a real dining reality
다음 주에 휴가 쓸 거니까 팀장님께 미리 말씀드렸어요.
I'll take leave next week, so I gave my team lead a heads-up in advance.
Real situation: 미리 + 말씀드리다 (humble form) for workplace advance notice
nuance: 미리 means doing something ahead of the relevant moment so you're ready when it arrives — its whole focus is the timing being early relative to a deadline or event. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing it with 우선 / 먼저 / 일단: 먼저 and 우선 mean 'first in a sequence or in priority' (do A before B), while 미리 means 'before the due time' (do it now so it's done early). 'I paid first' = 먼저 냈어요 (before others), but 'I paid in advance' = 미리 냈어요 (before the due date) — different ideas entirely. 미리 is native Korean, not Sino-Korean, and it glues onto preparation verbs: 미리 예약하다, 미리 준비하다, 미리 확인하다, 미리 알리다. Register is neutral and works in both polite and casual speech. Note the affectionate doubled 미리미리, which nags 'do it good and early.'

mistakes: Using 미리 for 'firstly in a sequence': 미리 이거부터 해요 is odd; for ordering steps you want 우선/먼저 이거부터 해요. 미리 only means 'ahead of the due time.'
Dropping it where the early timing is the point: 예약했어요 alone just says 'I booked'; 미리 예약했어요 adds the crucial 'ahead of time' nuance.
Saying 미리 전에 (advance + before) as a redundant pair under the influence of English 'beforehand in advance'; 미리 already contains 'before,' so just 미리 준비했어요.

english: first of all, first and foremost, to begin with
usage: 우선 loves -부터; 우선 이것부터 = let's start with this above all
Key noun built on 우선; 우선순위를 정하다 = set priorities
Polite way to settle someone before getting down to business
최 (most) + 우선; 안전이 최우선이에요 = safety is the top priority
examples: 우선 물 한 잔 드세요.
Have a glass of water first.
Simple: 우선 settling an immediate small thing before the rest
문제가 많지만 우선 급한 것부터 처리할게요.
There are many issues, but I'll handle the urgent ones first.
Everyday: 우선 + -부터 ordering tasks by priority at work
이사 오면 우선 전입신고부터 하셔야 해요.
When you move in, you must do the move-in report first of all.
Real situation: 우선 fronting the single most important admin step for residents
nuance: 우선 (優先, 優 'superior' + 先 'first') literally means 'take precedence,' so it marks what should come before everything else in importance, not merely in time. Compare 먼저 vs 우선: 먼저 is neutral sequence ('I'll go first / do this first'), while 우선 adds the flavor of priority and deliberate ranking ('first and foremost, before anything else'). Compare 우선 vs 일단: 일단 is 'for now, provisionally, then we'll see,' whereas 우선 ranks by importance. Compare 우선 vs 미리: 미리 is 'ahead of the deadline,' a totally different axis. The Sino-Korean root surfaces everywhere in daily life — 우선순위 (priority), 최우선 (top priority), 우선적으로 (preferentially) — so learning 우선 unlocks a whole word family. It pairs habitually with -부터 to pin the starting point. Register is neutral-to-formal and very common in workplace speech.

Using 우선 for plain 'then / next' steps in a list: 우선 ... 우선 ... sounds wrong; after the first item switch to 그다음에 / 그러고 나서.
Forgetting 우선 strongly prefers -부터: bare 우선 이거 해요 is weaker than the natural 우선 이거부터 해요.

english: for now, first (before deciding the rest), once
usage: The signature pattern; 일단 해 보고 결정하자 = let's just try it and then decide
일단 밥부터 먹자 = let's just eat first, sort the rest out later
Tentative acknowledgment that leaves room to revisit
일단 시작하면 = once you actually get started
examples: 일단 앉아서 얘기해요.
Let's just sit down first and talk.
Simple: 일단 settling one immediate step before the discussion
고민은 나중에 하고 일단 신청서부터 내요.
Worry about it later; for now, just submit the application first.
Everyday: 일단 deferring the deciding while taking one provisional action
집은 일단 계약했는데 이사 날짜는 아직 안 정했어요.
I went ahead and signed for the place for now, but haven't set the move date yet.
Real situation: 일단 = one thing settled provisionally while the rest stays open
nuance: 일단 (一旦, 一 'one' + 旦 'daybreak/moment') means 'for the moment, as a first provisional move' — you commit to one step now and leave the rest to be sorted out later. The defining flavor is tentativeness, which is the sharp line against 우선 and 미리. 우선 ranks by importance ('this matters most, do it first'); 일단 just says 'let's do something for now and see' with no claim about priority. 미리 means 'ahead of the deadline'; 일단 has nothing to do with deadlines. Its signature construction is 일단 ~하고 보자 / ~하고 보다 ('just do X first and see how it goes'), pure spoken Korean for deferring decisions. A second sense is conditional 'once': 일단 시작하면 끝까지 해야죠 ('once you start, you should finish'). Register is casual-to-neutral and extremely high-frequency in everyday speech.

Expecting it to mean 'in advance': that nuance belongs to 미리, never 일단.
Missing the 'once' sense and over-translating: 일단 도착하면 연락해 means 'once you arrive, contact me,' not 'for now arrive.'

usage: Classic 'on my way' text; 곧 도착해요 = I'll be there shortly
Announcing an event about to begin; 공연이 곧 시작합니다
to end soon / be over shortly
Reassurance; 거의 다 했어요, 곧 끝나요
Set adverb (esp. broadcasts/announcements): 곧이어 다음 순서입니다
examples: 봄이 곧 와요.
Spring is coming soon.
Simple: 곧 + a near-future event, forward-looking only
거의 다 왔어요, 곧 도착하니까 조금만 기다려요.
I'm almost there; I'll arrive soon, so wait just a bit.
Everyday: 곧 + 도착하다, the most relatable 'almost there' message
탑승을 곧 시작하겠습니다. 잠시만 기다려 주십시오.
Boarding will begin shortly. Please wait a moment.
Real situation: 곧 in a formal announcement register at the airport/station
nuance: 곧 means 'soon,' signaling that something will happen within a short time from the present. It strictly looks forward — 곧 can never describe the past. The key contrast is 곧 vs 금방: 금방 ('in a jiffy') is very casual and works both ways in time (it can even mean 'a moment ago' as in 금방 왔어요), while 곧 is cleaner, slightly more written/formal, and future-only, which is why station and airport announcements favor 곧. A second native-speaker pitfall is mixing 곧 (soon) with 이따가 (later today): 곧 means 'very shortly from now,' whereas 이따가 means 'later on, after some hours' — 곧 갈게요 ('I'm coming right away') is very different from 이따가 갈게요 ('I'll come by later'). 곧 is native Korean. The fixed compound 곧이어 ('coming up next') is worth memorizing as a unit.

mistakes: Using 곧 for the recent past ('a moment ago'): that is 방금 / 금방, while 곧 is strictly future. 곧 도착했어요 is wrong; say 방금 도착했어요.
Confusing 곧 (soon) with 곳 (place): they look and sound similar but are unrelated — 곧 = soon, 곳 = a place/spot.
Swapping 곧 and 이따가: 곧 = right away/shortly; 이따가 = later (in a few hours). Don't say 곧 만나요 when you mean 'see you later today.'

english: already (it's done and can't be changed)
usage: States a finished, irreversible fact; 이미 끝난 일이에요 = it's a done deal
이미 늦었어요 = there's no point now, the moment has passed
이미 알고 있었어요 = I knew it beforehand, this is no news
이미 결정된 상태예요 = it's already (been) decided, fixed now
examples: 그 영화는 이미 봤어요.
I've already seen that movie.
Simple: 이미 + completed action, a settled fact
전화했을 때는 이미 가게가 문을 닫았더라고요.
By the time I called, the store had already closed.
Everyday: 이미 with -더라고요 for a past-perfect 'it was already done' realization
환불하려고 했는데 이미 배송이 시작돼서 취소가 안 됐어요.
I tried to get a refund, but shipping had already started, so I couldn't cancel.
Real situation: 이미 marking an irreversible point in a process
nuance: 이미 means 'already,' emphasizing that an action or state is completed and now fixed — often colored by 'and there's no changing it now.' The sharp contrast every learner needs is 이미 vs 벌써. Both translate as 'already,' but 이미 is neutral and factual ('it is already done, that's just the situation'), while 벌써 adds emotional surprise that it happened so fast or so soon ('already?! that quick?'). 이미 끝났어요 = a calm statement of fact; 벌써 끝났어요?! = 'it's over already?!' with raised eyebrows. So choose 이미 when calmly noting that the moment/deadline has passed, and 벌써 when reacting to unexpected speed. 이미 is native Korean and is also future-blind: it only describes things already done, never things about to happen. It pairs naturally with completed clauses and with -더라고요, -았/었- past forms.

mistakes: Swapping it freely with 벌써: 이미 is neutral about timing, while 벌써 carries 'so soon?!' surprise. Use 이미 for a flat fact, 벌써 for astonishment.
Using it for the future: 이미 only describes things already done. 'It'll already be finished by then' needs a future-perfect feel like 그때면 끝나 있을 거예요, not 이미 + future.
Forcing English word order: in English 'already' floats around, but Korean 이미 sits before the verb/predicate it modifies — 이미 다 먹었어요, not 다 먹었어요 이미.

usage: 아까 말했잖아요 = I told you earlier (mild reminder)
아까부터 기다렸어요 = I've been waiting since earlier
아까 그 사람 = that person from before; refers back within today
earlier in the day / this morning
Pins 아까 to a rough part of today
examples: 아까 밥 먹었어요.
I ate a little while ago.
Simple: 아까 placing an action in the recent past today
아까 충전해 놨는데 벌써 배터리가 없어요.
I charged it earlier, but the battery's already dead.
Everyday: 아까 contrasting an earlier action with the present state
아까 회의 때 말씀하신 거 다시 한 번 설명해 주시겠어요?
Could you explain again what you mentioned earlier in the meeting?
Real situation: 아까 + 때 referencing a specific earlier moment today, polite register
nuance: 아까 refers to a short while earlier on the same day — broader than 'just now,' but always recent and never beyond today. The contrast learners most need is 아까 vs 방금: 방금 means literally seconds to a couple of minutes ago, while 아까 can stretch back a few hours (anywhere earlier today). 방금 도착했어요 = 'I arrived this second'; 아까 도착했어요 = 'I arrived a while ago (earlier today).' A second contrast is 아까 vs 전에: 전에 ('before / previously') is open-ended and can mean days, months, or years back, while 아까 is locked inside today. So use 아까 그거 ('that thing from earlier') only for something from the same day. 아까 is native Korean, casual-to-neutral in register, and combines productively with -부터 ('since earlier') and 그 + noun ('that ... from before').

mistakes: Using it for yesterday or longer ago: 아까 stays within today's recent past. For further back use 어제 / 전에 / 지난번에.
Treating it the same as 방금: 방금 = seconds ago, 아까 = a broader 'earlier today.' Don't say 아까 도착했어요 if you literally just walked in — that's 방금.
Pairing 아까 with the future: it is past-only. 'A bit later' is 이따가, not 아까.

usage: Reinforces the 'just now' sense; 지금 막 도착했어요
막 나가려던 참이었어요 = I was just on the point of leaving
막 먹다 = eat mindlessly; 막 쓰다 = use/spend carelessly
이제 막 시작했어요 = we've only just started
examples: 지금 막 일어났어요.
I just woke up (this second).
Simple: 지금 막 + past for an action completed an instant ago
문을 막 닫으려는데 누가 뛰어왔어요.
Right as I was about to close the door, someone came running.
Everyday: 막 + -려는데 marking the exact instant before another event
스트레스를 받으면 막 먹게 돼요.
When I'm stressed, I just end up eating mindlessly.
Real situation: 막 in the 'recklessly, without restraint' sense
nuance: 막 carries two everyday senses that context tells apart. (1) With a past tense or 참이다, it means 'just this very second' — even fresher and more immediate than 방금 — as in 지금 막 도착했어요 ('I arrived literally just now'). (2) In casual speech it also means doing something wildly, randomly, or without restraint, a shortening in feel of 마구: 막 먹다 (eat carelessly/a lot), 막 쓰다 (spend/use recklessly), 막 던지다 (throw all over the place). The pitfall for English speakers is hearing only the 'just' meaning and missing the 'recklessly' one, or vice versa — the following verb and tone decide it: 막 + past = time; 막 + ongoing careless action = manner. 막 is native Korean and very colloquial; the manner sense in particular sounds casual, so go easy on it in formal settings. It frequently teams up with 지금, 이제, and -려던 참이다 for the time reading.

Forgetting it usually leans on 지금 / 이제 or 참이다 for the time sense: bare 막 도착했어요 is fine, but 지금 막 / 이제 막 / 막 ~려던 참 sound more natural and unambiguous.
Using the careless 막 in polite/formal speech: 막 in the 'wildly' sense is colloquial and can sound crude — soften or avoid it when being formal.

usage: 방금 도착했어요 = I got here only seconds ago
방금 뭐라고 했어요? = asking to repeat what was said a second ago
Common variant emphasizing the very recent instant
방금까지 여기 있었어요 = it was right here until seconds ago
examples: 방금 도착했어요.
I arrived just now.
Simple: 방금 + past for an action seconds old
방금 주문하신 음료 나왔습니다.
The drink you just ordered is ready.
Everyday: 방금 in a cafe, an order only moments old, polite -습니다 register
방금까지 옆에 있었는데 잠깐 사이에 어디 갔지?
They were right beside me until just now; where'd they go in that instant?
Real situation: 방금까지 emphasizing 'up until seconds ago'
nuance: 방금 (方今, 方 'just/at the time' + 今 'now') is the tightest 'recent past' word, pointing to something that happened only seconds to a couple of minutes ago. The contrast learners need most is 방금 vs 아까: 방금 is 'this very moment past,' while 아까 stretches to 'earlier today' (potentially hours back). 방금 나갔어요 = 'they left seconds ago'; 아까 나갔어요 = 'they left a while ago.' Compare also 방금 vs 막: both can mean 'just now,' but 막 emphasizes the instantaneous edge ('right as it happened') and pairs with 지금/참이다, whereas 방금 is a standalone time word and a touch more neutral. Because of its Sino-Korean root, the variant 방금 전(에) ('just a moment before') is common. 방금 is strictly immediate past — never future. Register is neutral and fits both casual and polite speech, which is why staff use it (방금 주문하신…).

Using it for the future: 방금 is strictly the immediate past, never 'in a moment' — that's 곧 / 이따가.
Over-distinguishing from 막 when they overlap: in many sentences 방금 도착했어요 and (지금) 막 도착했어요 are interchangeable, but pick 막 when you want the 'right as it happened' edge.

english: in the meantime, all this while, during that time
usage: to have been well all this time
그동안 잘 지냈어요? = standard catch-up greeting after a gap
to be thankful for everything up to now
그동안 고마웠어요 = gratitude covering a whole past stretch (often a farewell)
그동안의 노력 = the effort (made) over all that time; noun-modifying use
그동안 못 만났네요 = we couldn't meet all this time
examples: 그동안 바빴어요.
I was busy all this while.
Simple: 그동안 covering an elapsed stretch up to now
오랜만이에요, 그동안 어떻게 지냈어요?
Long time no see; how have you been all this while?
Everyday: 그동안 framing the whole gap since you last met
그동안 모아 둔 돈으로 드디어 전셋집을 구했어요.
With the money I'd saved up all this time, I finally found a jeonse place.
Real situation: 그동안 referring to an extended past saving period
nuance: 그동안 (그 'that' + 동안 'duration/while') means 'during that time / all this while,' referring to a stretch of time spanning a known gap and usually leading up to now. It's the backbone of catching-up greetings (그동안 잘 지냈어요?) and farewell thanks (그동안 고마웠어요). The first pitfall is treating it as a single point: 그동안 is always a span, unlike 그때 ('at that time / that moment'). The second is direction — 그동안 vs 당분간: 그동안 looks back over time that has elapsed, while 당분간 ('for the time being') looks forward from now. So 'thanks for everything up to now' = 그동안 고마웠어요, but 'I'll rest for a while going forward' = 당분간 쉴게요. Grammatically 그동안 is flexible: it works as an adverb (그동안 바빴어요) and, with -의, as a noun modifier (그동안의 노력). Register is neutral and warm; the greeting use is everyday-polite.

Using it where you mean a specific past day: for 'the other day / last time' use 지난번 / 저번에, not 그동안.

english: for the time being, for a while (from now)
usage: to rest for a while (going forward)
당분간 쉬려고요 = I plan to take a break for the time being
당분간 못 만나요 = we can't meet for a while (a temporary inability)
당분간 외식 안 할 거예요 = I won't eat out for the time being
for the time being at least
Softens to 'at least for now'; implies it may change later
examples: 당분간 바쁠 거예요.
I'll be busy for the time being.
Simple: 당분간 + future, a temporary state ahead
돈을 모아야 해서 당분간 여행은 안 가려고요.
I need to save money, so I'm not going to travel for the time being.
Everyday: 당분간 + future restraint a budgeting resident relates to
이직 준비 때문에 당분간 약속을 좀 줄이려고 해요.
Because I'm prepping for a job change, I'm going to cut back on plans for a while.
Real situation: 당분간 marking a temporary phase ahead with -려고 해요
nuance: 당분간 (當分間, roughly 當 'this present' + 分 'portion' + 間 'interval' — 'for this present interval') means 'for the time being': a limited stretch starting now and running into the near future, with a built-in implication that it's temporary and will change. The defining contrast is 당분간 vs 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now, for a while'), 그동안 points back over elapsed time. So 'I'll lie low for a while' = 당분간 조용히 지낼게요, but 'thanks for everything until now' = 그동안 고마웠어요. A second pitfall is using it for permanent states: 당분간 inherently signals 'this won't last forever.' It pairs naturally with future-plan endings (-(으)려고요, -ㄹ 거예요) and negatives of restraint (못, 안 ... -ㄹ 거예요), and it's often softened to 당분간은. Register is neutral and very common in everyday explanations of temporary plans.

mistakes: Confusing it with 그동안: 당분간 points forward ('from now for a while'), while 그동안 points back over time that has passed.
Using it for permanent states: 당분간 implies the situation is temporary and expected to change. For 'forever / from now on for good' use 앞으로 (계속) / 영원히.
Pairing it with a plain past tense: since 당분간 looks forward, it wants future/intention forms — say 당분간 쉴 거예요 / 쉬려고요, not 당분간 쉬었어요.

english: in that short time, in the blink of an eye (so fast)
usage: did you ~ it all in that short time?
그새 다 먹었어요? = you finished it all that fast?! (surprise)
그새 또 비가 오네요 = it's raining again already, in no time
to forget in that short while
그새 잊어버렸어요 = it slipped my mind that quickly
can't wait even that brief moment
Noun use of 그새 (that short interval); 그새를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that bit
examples: 그새 다 컸네요.
They've grown so much in no time.
Simple: 그새 + change, with built-in 'so fast!' surprise
잠깐 화장실 다녀왔는데 그새 자리가 없어졌어요.
I just popped to the restroom, and in that short time my seat was gone.
Everyday: 그새 stressing how fast things changed in a brief absence
분명히 여기 뒀는데 그새 어디 갔지?
I clearly put it right here; where'd it go in that instant?
Real situation: 그새 marking a baffling change over a brief moment
nuance: 그새 is a contracted, set form of 그 사이 ('that interval/gap') and means 'in that short while' — almost always carrying a tone of surprise that so much changed in so little time. The contrast learners must keep straight is 그새 vs 그동안: 그동안 is a neutral, often longish stretch ('all this while'), while 그새 specifically flags a surprisingly short interval ('that quick?!'). 그동안 잘 지냈어요? is a calm catch-up; 그새 다 먹었어? is astonishment at speed. It can also work as a noun for that brief stretch itself (그새를 못 참다, 'can't even wait that little bit'). 그새 is native Korean and decidedly casual/spoken — great for reacting to quick changes among friends, less so in formal writing, where 그 사이에 / 그 짧은 사이에 reads better. Note the spelling: keep it as the single set word 그새 to carry the 'so fast!' nuance.

Losing the surprise nuance by over-formalizing: in neutral writing 그 사이에 is fine, but the punchy 'so fast!' feeling lives in the set spoken form 그새.

english: long ago, sooner (should have done it earlier)
usage: 진작 할걸 = I should've done it long ago (self-regret)
진작 말했어야지 = you should've said so sooner (mild reproach)
Wishing the knowledge had come earlier
Emphatic variant; 진작에 했어야죠 = you really should've done it long ago
examples: 진작 말하지 그랬어요.
You should've told me sooner.
Simple: 진작 + -지 그랬어요, gentle 'why didn't you earlier' reproach
이렇게 쉬운 걸 진작 할걸 그랬어요.
I should have done something this easy long ago.
Everyday: 진작 + -ㄹ걸 그랬다 expressing regret over delaying
맛집인 줄 알았으면 진작 와 봤을 텐데.
If I'd known it was this good, I'd have come sooner.
Real situation: 진작 in an -았/었을 텐데 hypothetical regret about timing
nuance: 진작 means 'sooner / long ago,' but — and this is the whole point — it almost always carries regret or mild reproach that something wasn't done earlier than it actually was. It is not a neutral time word. The contrast learners must internalize is 진작 vs 전에 / 이미: 전에 ('before') and 이미 ('already') are neutral statements of fact, whereas 진작 is loaded with hindsight ('ah, if only it had been done earlier'). So 'I told you before' = 전에 말했어요 (neutral), but 'you should've told me sooner!' = 진작 말하지 (regretful). Because of this emotional core, 진작 habitually pairs with regret/counterfactual endings: -ㄹ걸 (그랬다), -았/었어야지, -았/었으면 ... -ㄹ 텐데. The emphatic variant 진작에 piles on the 'way earlier' feeling. 진작 is native-feeling, casual-to-neutral, and lands flat or even rude if you strip the regret framing.

So 'I told you before' = 전에 말했어요 (neutral), but 'you should've told me sooner!' = 진작 말하지 (regretful).
